Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current Foundation Models trained on Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are severely constrained by limited context windows, typically restricting input to a small fraction of a patient's medical history. This truncation is particularly detrimental for patients with complex, chronic conditions whose records span tens of thousands of clinical events. The dominant Transformer architectures cannot feasibly scale to these full longitudinal timelines due to the quadratic computational cost of self-attention. Furthermore, applying standard Natural Language Processing (NLP) strategies to EHRs often neglects the unique stochastic properties of clinical data, such as irregular time intervals between visits and the artificial repetition of data due to administrative "copy-forwarding."

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that emerging **subquadratic sequence modeling architectures** (such as State Space Models or implicit long convolutions) can enable the efficient processing of full-length longitudinal EHRs, surpassing the limitations of Transformer-based models. We postulate that extending the context window will not only improve general predictive performance by capturing long-term dependencies but will also provide specific robustness against unique EHR noise artifacts. Specifically, a longer view of the patient timeline should allow the model to better filter redundant "copy-forwarded" tokens and better interpolate across irregular temporal gaps.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

**Data Representation and Tokenization**
We propose to treat the EHR as a chronological sequence of discrete clinical events. Rather than using subword tokenization common in NLP, we will map structured clinical codes (diagnoses, medications, procedures, labs) directly to a vocabulary of tokens. To handle the temporal aspect, we will integrate positional information that reflects the sequence order, while implicitly requiring the model to learn the irregular time lapses between events through the data distribution.

**Architectural Investigation**
We will implement and train subquadratic architectures designed for linear-time sequence modeling. These models replace the attention mechanism with state-space transitions or long convolutions, allowing us to drastically increase the context length without incurring quadratic memory or compute penalties. We will compare these against standard Transformer and Decoder-only baselines to isolate the impact of architecture versus context length.

**Training Strategy**
The models will be pretrained using a standard autoregressive next-token prediction objective. The training loop will be designed to ingest sequences significantly longer than the standard limitations, aiming to cover entire patient histories in a single forward pass.

**Domain-Specific Robustness Analysis**
Instead of treating the data solely as text, we will design our evaluation framework to test the models' ability to handle non-linguistic data properties. We will theoretically analyze the models' internal states to understand how they manage:
1.  **High Repetition:** Distinguishing between meaningful recurrence of disease and administrative repetition.
2.  **Temporal Irregularity:** Handling variance in the "physical time" distance between adjacent tokens.
3.  **Entropy Shift:** Adapting to the increasing complexity of clinical events as a patient ages (disease progression), which contrasts with the decreasing entropy typically seen in long natural language documents.

## Expected Contribution
This project intends to establish the viability of subquadratic architectures for structured clinical data, potentially shifting the paradigm away from Attention-based models for long sequences. By demonstrating that long-context models are more robust to the specific noise and irregularity of EHRs, we aim to provide a theoretical justification for prioritizing "whole-patient" modeling over short-window snapshots. This will serve as a foundational blueprint for adapting sequence models to domains characterized by continuous, irregular, and repetitive event streams.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a systematic evaluation of the effect of context length on modeling Electronic Health Record (EHR) data using various foundation model architectures.

### Datasets
*   **Pretraining Dataset:** Deidentified longitudinal EHR data formatted under the OMOP Common Data Model (EHR-OMOP).
    *   **Source:** Academic medical center.
    *   **Training Split:** 2.5 million patients (3.5 billion clinical events).
    *   **Validation Split:** 0.5 million patients.
    *   **Patient Statistics:** Average patient had 1,364 total events and 237 unique events.
*   **Evaluation Benchmark:** EHRSHOT clinical prediction benchmark.
    *   **Size:** 7,000 patients.
    *   **Tasks:** 14 binary classification tasks.
    *   **Settings:** Zero-shot, Few-shot (k=8, 16, 32, 64, 128), and All-data (Full Fine-tuning).

### Data Processing & Tokenization
*   **Vocabulary:** 39,811 tokens (top frequently occurring codes).
*   **Tokenization Strategy:**
    *   Unique codes mapped to unique tokens.
    *   Categorical values mapped to unique tokens.
    *   Numerical values deciled (0-9) and mapped to unique tokens per decile.
    *   Special tokens included: [BOS], [EOS], [UNK], [SEP], [PAD], [CLS], [MASK].
    *   Total vocabulary size: 39,818.
*   **Artificial Time Tokens (ATT):** We experimented with injecting artificial tokens representing time intervals (days, weeks, months, long-term) between visits, enclosed by Visit Start (VS) and Visit End (VE) tokens.

### Architectures & Context Lengths
We evaluated four model architectures at the ~120 million parameter scale.
*   **Architectures:**
    1.  **GPT:** Transformer-based, absolute positional embeddings.
    2.  **Llama:** Transformer-based, rotary positional embeddings (RoPE).
    3.  **Mamba:** State Space Model (Subquadratic).
    4.  **Hyena:** Long Convolution (Subquadratic).
*   **Context Lengths tested:**
    *   Transformers (GPT, Llama): 512, 1024 (1k), 2048 (2k), 4096 (4k).
    *   Subquadratic (Mamba, Hyena): 1024 (1k), 4096 (4k), 8192 (8k), 16384 (16k).

### Training Details
*   **Objective:** Autoregressive next-token prediction with cross-entropy loss.
*   **Training Duration:** 2 billion tokens.
*   **Hardware:** Clusters of NVIDIA V100s, with limited A100/H100 usage.
*   **Optimizer:** AdamW ($\beta_1=0.9, \beta_2=0.95, \lambda=0.1$).
*   **Learning Rate:** Sweep performed between 1e-6 and 1e-3; settled on 2e-4.
*   **Schedule:** Linear warm-up for 40,000 steps, then decay to 1e-5.
*   **Batch Size:** Gradient accumulation used for effective batch size of 65,536 tokens per step.

### Evaluation Metrics
*   **Primary:** Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC).
*   **Secondary:** Brier Score (for evaluating robustness to repetition/irregularity).
*   **Analysis Metrics:** Perplexity (PPL), n-gram repetition rate, standard deviation of inter-event times.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

### Model Performance and Context Length
*   **Observation:** Mamba with a 16k token context length achieved the highest average AUROC (0.807) across all 14 tasks, surpassing the prior state-of-the-art model (CLMBR-t-base, 0.777) by 0.03 points.
*   **Observation:** Model performance for Mamba and Llama generally improved as context length increased.
*   **Observation:** Hyena performance degraded sharply when context length exceeded 4k tokens.
*   **Observation:** GPT performance with respect to context length was inconsistent, likely due to absolute positional embeddings.
*   **Observation:** The use of Artificial Time Tokens (ATT) resulted in slightly worse performance compared to models trained without ATTs, with standard Mamba-16k remaining the top performer.

### EHR-Specific Data Properties
*   **Observation (Repetitiveness):** EHR data exhibited significantly higher n-gram repetition rates (n=1,2,3,4) compared to natural language (WikiText-103).
*   **Observation (Repetitiveness Impact):** Increased patient timeline repetitiveness correlated with degraded model performance (higher Brier scores) for all models. However, longer context models (Mamba-16k, Llama-4k) achieved lower Brier scores across all quartiles of repetitiveness compared to their shorter context counterparts.
*   **Observation (Irregularity):** EHR data showed high irregularity in time intervals between events, with standard deviations ranging from $10^7$ to $10^8$ seconds (approx. 115 days to 3.2 years).
*   **Observation (Irregularity Impact):** Increased irregularity in inter-event times correlated with degraded model performance. Longer context models consistently outperformed shorter versions across all irregularity quartiles.
*   **Observation (Disease Progression):** Median perplexity increased for tokens later in patient timelines, contrasting with natural language where perplexity typically decreases as context grows.
*   **Observation (Disease Progression Impact):** Longer context Mamba and Llama models achieved lower perplexities across all token positions compared to shorter contexts, suggesting better handling of increasing complexity.
*   **Observation (GPT Specifics):** GPT models using absolute positional embeddings showed perplexity spikes at later token positions. Replacing these with rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) mitigated the spikes but preserved the trend of increasing perplexity over time.

### Few-Shot Learning
*   **Observation:** Performance (AUROC) consistently improved as the number of few-shot examples ($k$) increased from 8 to 128 across all task groups.
*   **Observation:** Mamba-16k and Llama-4k frequently achieved the highest AUROC scores in few-shot settings, particularly at higher $k$ values (64 and 128).

### Zero-Shot Learning
*   **Observation:** Zero-shot performance for all evaluated models (Mamba, Llama) significantly lagged behind few-shot and fine-tuned performance.
*   **Observation:** No zero-shot model outperformed the prior fine-tuned SOTA (CLMBR-t-base) on the evaluated tasks.

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).

* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are inherently longitudinal, consisting of chronological sequences of clinical events that span a patient's lifetime. For patients with complex medical histories—often the individuals at highest risk—these sequences can exceed tens of thousands of events. However, current state-of-the-art Foundation Models (FMs) for EHRs primarily rely on Transformer-based architectures (e.g., BERT, GPT). Due to the quadratic computational complexity of the self-attention mechanism ($O(n^2)$), these models are typically constrained to short context windows (e.g., 512 tokens).

This technical limitation forces a truncation of patient history, preventing models from referencing and reasoning over long-term temporal dependencies. Consequently, the distinct structural properties of EHR data—specifically long-term irregularity in event timing and high repetition—are poorly modeled. There is currently no systematic framework for applying subquadratic architectures to longitudinal EHR data to overcome these context limits.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that shifting from quadratic Transformer architectures to subquadratic, long-context architectures (specifically State Space Models and Long Convolutional models) will enable the ingestion of full patient timelines (up to 16k tokens or more) without prohibitive computational costs.

We posit that extending the context length will theoretically improve the representation of patient states by capturing three specific properties of clinical data that short-context models miss:
1.  **Copy-forwarding:** Handling the artificial repetition of diagnosis codes over long periods.
2.  **Irregularity:** Modeling the wide variance in time intervals between clinical events (ranging from days to years).
3.  **Disease Progression:** Accounting for the increasing complexity (entropy) of clinical events as a patient ages.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of EHR Data
We will model the EHR as a sequence of discrete tokens derived from clinical events. Let a dataset consist of $n$ patients $X = \{ X_1, ..., X_n \}$. For each patient $i$, the structured EHR data is a sequence of chronologically ordered events $X_{ij}$:
$$ X_i = \{ X_{i1}, X_{i2}, ..., X_{i|X_i|} \} $$
Each event is a tuple $X_{ij} = (t_{ij}, c_{ij}, v_{ij})$, where $t_{ij}$ is the timestamp, $c_{ij} \in \mathcal{C}$ is a code from a medical ontology, and $v_{ij}$ is an associated value (categorical or numeric).

### 2. Tokenization and Embedding Strategy
To convert the event stream into a sequence of tokens $T_i$ suitable for autoregressive modeling, we will implement a mapping function $g$ that handles the heterogeneous nature of $v_{ij}$.

Let $D: \mathcal{C} \times \mathcal{V}_n \to \{x \in \mathbb{Z} \mid 0 \leq x \leq 9\}$ be a deciling function for numerical values. Let $G(\cdot)$ map inputs to a unique integer in the vocabulary. The tokenization function $g$ will be defined as:
$$ g(X_{ij}) = \begin{cases} G(c_{ij}) & \text{if } v_{ij} = \emptyset \\ G(c_{ij}, v_{ij}) & \text{if } v_{ij} \text{ is categorical} \\ G(c_{ij}, D(c_{ij}, v_{ij})) & \text{if } v_{ij} \text{ is numeric} \end{cases} $$
We will construct a vocabulary consisting of the top $\approx 40,000$ most informative tokens based on occurrence frequency in the training corpus.

### 3. Model Architectures
We will design and train four distinct architectures to isolate the effect of context length and architectural inductive bias. All models will be standardized to approximately 120 million parameters.

**A. Transformer Baselines (GPT and Llama)**
We will implement standard causal Transformers. For the Llama variant, we will replace absolute positional embeddings with Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) to better handle relative distances in clinical sequences. RoPE encodes position $i$ by rotating the query $q$ and key $k$ vectors:
$$ \mathrm{RoPE}(q, k, i) = \cos(i\theta)q + \sin(i\theta)k $$
where $\theta$ is the frequency parameter. Due to quadratic scaling, these models will be trained with context lengths $L \in \{512, 1k, 2k, 4k\}$.

**B. Mamba (State Space Model)**
To test linear-time sequence modeling, we will implement the Mamba architecture. This relies on a selective state space model defined by the continuous-time evolution:
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{t+1} &= A\mathbf{x}_t + B\mathbf{u}_t \\ \mathbf{y}_t &= C\mathbf{x}_t + D\mathbf{u}_t \end{aligned} $$
Here, $\mathbf{x}_t$ is the hidden state, $\mathbf{u}_t$ is the input token embedding, and $\mathbf{y}_t$ is the output. $A, B, C, D$ are learned matrices. This formulation allows for context lengths $L \in \{1k, 4k, 8k, 16k\}$ with linear computational scaling.

**C. Hyena (Long Convolutions)**
We will implement Hyena, which replaces attention with implicit long convolutions and multiplicative gating. The core operation for input sequence $\mathbf{x}(t)$ is:
$$ \mathbf{y}(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{L-1} \mathbf{h}(i) \cdot \mathbf{x}(t-i) $$
where $\mathbf{h}(i)$ is a learned convolution filter of length $L$. This is followed by a gating mechanism:
$$ \mathbf{z}(t) = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_1 \cdot \mathbf{y}(t)) \odot (\mathbf{W}_2 \cdot \mathbf{y}(t)) $$
where $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication.

### 4. Representation Learning and Inference
We will train all models using an autoregressive next-token prediction objective. For downstream clinical prediction tasks, we will extract a fixed-size patient representation $R_i$ by pooling the outputs of the model $m$ over the last $L$ tokens of the patient timeline:
$$ R_i = \operatorname{mean}(m(\{ T_{i, |T_i|-L}, ..., T_{i|T_i|} \})) $$
This representation $R_i$ will serve as the input to a linear classifier for binary prediction tasks.

### 5. Quantifying EHR-Specific Properties
To theoretically validate why long-context models may succeed or fail, we will formalize three metrics specific to clinical data:

1.  **Repetitiveness (Copy-Forwarding):** We will define the $n$-gram repetition rate ($RR_n$) to measure redundant coding:
    $$ \mathrm{RR}_n(x) = \frac{\sum_{u \in \mathcal{U}(x)} \mathbb{I}[C(u, x) > 1]}{|\mathcal{U}(x)|} $$
    where $\mathcal{U}(x)$ is the set of unique $n$-grams and $C(u, x)$ is the count of $n$-gram $u$ in sequence $x$.

2.  **Irregularity:** We will quantify the variation in time intervals between events. Let $\Delta t_{ij} = t_{i(j+1)} - t_{ij}$. We define irregularity $I_{\sigma}^{(i)}$ as the standard deviation of these intervals:
    $$ I_{\sigma}^{(i)} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|X_i|-1} \sum_{j=1}^{|X_i|-1} (\Delta t_{ij} - \mu_i)^2} $$

3.  **Disease Complexity:** We will measure the perplexity of tokens as a function of their position in the patient timeline to test the hypothesis that disease complexity increases over time (unlike natural language, where context lowers perplexity).

## Expected Contribution
This project will provide the first rigorous evaluation of subquadratic architectures (Mamba, Hyena) on longitudinal EHR data. We expect to demonstrate that:
1.  Extending context windows beyond the standard 512 tokens significantly improves predictive performance for clinical tasks.
2.  Subquadratic architectures can match or exceed the performance of Transformers on EHR data while enabling much longer efficient context.
3.  Long-context models are theoretically better equipped to handle the high noise (repetition) and temporal irregularity inherent in real-world clinical data compared to their short-context counterparts.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
